title: Local Dephasing Sustains Continuous Time Crystals in a Spin-1/2 Ensemble
problem: Pure dephasing destroys single-spin coherence and is normally counted as loss. In a fully connected ferromagnetic spin-\(1/2\) ensemble with local decay, can dephasing instead be what keeps a collective oscillation going, a continuous time crystal under time-independent dynamics?
result: Yes. An exact operator identity shows that dephasing feeds energy into the transverse interaction, which local decay removes with a delay of order \(1/\Gamma_1\). In homogeneous mean field there is no periodic orbit without dephasing, and on a periodic orbit the delayed feedback exactly pays for the transverse damping. Liouvillian spectra for \(N=80\)–\(300\) show oscillatory decay rates falling as \(N^{-0.32}\) and \(N^{-0.46}\), with frequencies approaching the mean-field values.
significance: It turns a ubiquitous decoherence channel into a control parameter for autonomous temporal order. The identity gives a testable amplitude–phase relation between energy and magnetization in every oscillatory mode, which can be checked beyond all-to-all models. The oscillating state also takes part in metastable switching between two stationary states.
limitations: The necessity proof holds in homogeneous mean field. At finite \(N\) the evidence is power-law fits over \(N\le300\), not a proof that decay rates vanish. The limit cycle coexists with two stable fixed points, so whether oscillations appear depends on the initial state. Fluctuations and photon-counting readout are treated with a semiclassical diffusion model rather than exact quantum trajectories, and no experiment is reported.
summary_basis: Description based on the full text of the linked arXiv version, read 2026-10-25; equations follow the paper’s notation.

methods.technique: Exact energy balance from an observable that commutes with the Hamiltonian
methods.explanation: An observable that commutes with \(H\) changes only through the dissipators, so its Heisenberg equation is exact at any \(N\) and often closes on a few operators. Here it separates energy loss from a dephasing-driven source and constrains every Liouvillian mode.
math: With \(Q_N=h_z(M_z+I)-JU_N\) and \([H,Q_N]=0\), \(\mathcal L^\dagger Q_N=\mathcal L^\dagger_{\rm diss}Q_N\). Local decay gives \(\mathcal L^\dagger_{\rm diss}(M_z+I)=-\Gamma_1(M_z+I)\), and each product \(\sigma_i^x\sigma_j^x\) of distinct spins decays at \(2\Gamma_2\), so \(\mathcal L^\dagger_{\rm diss}U_N=-2\Gamma_2U_N\). Hence \(\mathcal L^\dagger Q_N=-\Gamma_1Q_N+(2\Gamma_2-\Gamma_1)JU_N\), and \(2\Gamma_2-\Gamma_1=4\gamma_\phi\).

For a right eigenmode \(\mathcal LR_k=\lambda_kR_k\) with \(\operatorname{Tr}R_k=0\), projecting the identity gives \(\lambda_kq_k=-\Gamma_1q_k+4J\gamma_\phi u_k\), so \(q_k/u_k=4J\gamma_\phi/(\Gamma_1+\lambda_k)\) with \(q_k=\operatorname{Tr}(Q_NR_k)\) and \(u_k=\operatorname{Tr}(U_NR_k)\). As \(\kappa_k\to0\) this becomes the harmonic response \(4J\gamma_\phi/(\Gamma_1+i\nu)\).

Editorial check: integrating the mean-field equations at the Fig. 1 parameters, \(\dot Q=-\Gamma_1Q+4J\gamma_\phi m_x^2\) holds to \(10^{-13}\) along the trajectory. With \(\gamma_\phi=0\) the state settles at \(m_z=-0.5\); with \(\gamma_\phi=1.5\), \(m_z\) keeps oscillating between \(-0.63\) and \(-0.38\) at late times.
methods.transfer: In an open many-body model, look for a conserved quantity shifted by a constant so that the dissipators map it into a small operator set. The resulting identity gives exact finite-\(N\) relations between eigenmode projections and between correlation functions, which also check numerics. It needs dissipators that do not generate a growing operator hierarchy.

methods.technique: Cycle work of a lagged feedback variable
methods.explanation: To decide whether a damped oscillator coupled to a relaxing variable can sustain a periodic orbit, multiply its equation by the velocity and integrate over a period. Conservative terms drop out, so damping must be paid by feedback work, and that work is nonzero only if the feedback lags.
math: Eliminating \(m_y=-(\dot m_x+\Gamma_2m_x)/h_z\) and \(m_z=(Q+Jm_x^2)/h_z-1\) gives \[\ddot m_x+2\Gamma_2\dot m_x=-(h_z^2+\Gamma_2^2-2h_zJ)m_x-2J^2m_x^3-2JQm_x.\] Multiplying by \(\dot m_x\) and integrating over a period gives \(2\Gamma_2\oint\dot m_x^2\,dt=-J\oint Q\,d(m_x^2)\). If \(\gamma_\phi=0\), \(Q\to0\), the right side vanishes and \(m_x\) is constant.

With \(u=m_x^2\) and \(\dot Q=-\Gamma_1Q+4J\gamma_\phi u\), integration by parts gives \[-J\langle Q\dot u\rangle=J\langle\dot Qu\rangle=\frac{\langle\dot Q(\dot Q+\Gamma_1Q)\rangle}{4\gamma_\phi}=\frac{\langle\dot Q^2\rangle}{4\gamma_\phi},\] since \(\langle Q\dot Q\rangle=0\) over a period. The work is strictly positive unless \(Q\) is constant. If \(Q\) were proportional to \(u\) at every instant, the loop would have zero area.

Editorial check: on the \(\gamma_\phi=1.5\) orbit (period \(T\approx0.29\,T_1\)), averaging over 33 whole periods gives \(2\Gamma_2\langle\dot m_x^2\rangle\), \(-J\langle Q\dot u\rangle\) and \(\langle\dot Q^2\rangle/(4\gamma_\phi)\) all equal to 420.99. The charging–loss balance \(\Gamma_1\langle Q\rangle=4J\gamma_\phi\langle m_x^2\rangle=39.93\) holds as well.
methods.transfer: For any oscillator coupled to a slowly relaxing variable (temperature, population, cavity field), this energy method gives a necessary condition for limit cycles: a nonzero source and a finite relaxation time. The \(\langle\dot Q^2\rangle\) form fixes the sign without solving for the orbit. It does not prove that the cycle exists or say which initial states reach it.

methods_source_section: Section III.1 (Eqs. 7–8); Section III.2–III.3 (Eqs. 9–18); Section IV.2 (Eqs. 24–27)
methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: The model is \(H=\tfrac{h_z}{2}\sum_i\sigma_i^z-\tfrac{J}{N}\sum_{i<j}\sigma_i^x\sigma_j^x\), with each spin subject to decay \(\gamma\mathcal D[\sigma_i^-]\) and pure dephasing \(\gamma_\phi\mathcal D[\sigma_i^z]\), so \(\Gamma_1=\gamma\) and \(\Gamma_2=\gamma/2+2\gamma_\phi\). In homogeneous mean field the Bloch vector obeys nonlinear Bloch equations. At \(J=h_z\approx105\,\Gamma_1\) and from the same initial state, the magnetization relaxes when \(\gamma_\phi=0\) and oscillates indefinitely when \(\gamma_\phi=1.5\,\Gamma_1\). Two symmetry-related fixed points \(F_\pm\) exist when \(2h_zJ>h_z^2+\Gamma_2^2\), and linearization shows they are always stable. The limit cycle therefore does not come from a Hopf bifurcation but coexists with them, and the outcome depends on the basin of the initial state.

The mechanism comes from the shifted energy \(Q_N=2H/N+h_zI\). Because it commutes with \(H\), only the dissipators change it, and \(\mathcal L^\dagger Q_N=-\Gamma_1Q_N+4J\gamma_\phi U_N\), where \(U_N\) is the transverse pair correlation. Ferromagnetically aligned transverse spins lower the interaction energy, and dephasing destroys that alignment, so it raises the energy. In mean field \(\dot Q=-\Gamma_1Q+4J\gamma_\phi m_x^2\). Eliminating \(m_y\) and \(m_z\) leaves a damped nonlinear oscillator for \(m_x\) with an extra force \(-2JQm_x\). Without dephasing \(Q\) decays to zero, and an energy argument over one period forces \(\dot m_x\equiv0\), so no periodic orbit exists.

Charging alone does not explain motion, because charging and loss can also balance at a fixed point. What matters is that \(Q\) follows \(m_x^2\) through a memory kernel \(e^{-\Gamma_1s}\), so each harmonic lags by \(\arctan(\nu/\Gamma_1)\). The lag makes the orbit enclose an area in the \((m_x^2,Q)\) plane, and the feedback work around this loop equals \(\langle\dot Q^2\rangle/(4\gamma_\phi)>0\). It exactly balances the damping \(2\Gamma_2\oint\dot m_x^2\,dt\). An instantaneous response would retrace a line and do no work.

Beyond mean field, the Liouvillian is diagonalized in Dicke blocks for \(N=80\)–\(300\). The odd and even oscillatory branches become longer lived (\(\kappa\propto N^{-0.323}\), \(N^{-0.458}\)), their frequencies approach \(\Omega\) and \(2\Omega\), and the per-spin oscillatory weights in stationary correlations stay of comparable size. Projecting the identity onto an eigenmode gives \(q_k/u_k=4J\gamma_\phi/(\Gamma_1+\lambda_k)\), the quantum version of the mean-field lag. Semiclassical trajectories at \(N=10^5\) show oscillatory episodes interrupted by stays near \(F_\pm\), about 13% of the time, followed by reactivation. Simulated photon counting at efficiency 0.3 resolves the \(2\Omega\) peak from \(N=10^5\) upward.
